Zoom in on a local part of the body, and the pattern of blood vessels will look like the pattern for the entire body.

choices.text: The seeds of several subspecies of maple tree resemble one another in shape despite differences in size.
choices.explanation:
This does not provide the key idea that "zooming in on a small part looks like the big thing".

These are all small parts. The seed of this subspecies of maple tree resembles the seed of that subspecies of maple tree, even though one is bigger than the other.

While this answer implies that the smaller seed resembles the bigger seed, that's not the same as a Part resembles Whole relationship.

choices.text: The florets composing a cauliflower head resemble the entire cauliflower head.
choices.explanation:
This provides the key idea that "zooming in on a small part looks like the big thing".

Zoom in on a floret within the cauliflower, and it looks like the entire head of cauliflower.

questions.prompt: In the first paragraph, the explanation of how a Koch curve is generated serves primarily to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
When we do Local Purpose questions (in order to / serves to / primarily to), we generally expect the correct answer to reinforce the framing idea that comes right before the lines the question stem is pointing us to.

Is there some broader setup idea that prefaces the discussion of how the Koch curve is generated?

Yes, the 3rd sentence says,
*examining the Koch curve **provides some insight** into fractal geometry*.

So we know the author's purpose in explaining the Koch curve is to provide some insight into fractal geometry, potentially emphasizing the signature quality we heard about in the 2nd sentence (self-similarity).

choices.text: show how fractal geometry can be reduced to traditional geometry
choices.explanation:
This sounds sort of like the opposite of what we were looking for, which was "to provide some insight into fractal geometry".

It wouldn't be much of an insight to say, "It's really just traditional geometry".

choices.text: give an example of a natural form that can be described by fractal geometry
choices.explanation: The Koch curve is a mathematical construction described by explicit repeated rules. The passage does not present it as a naturally occurring form. The process is not random.

choices.text: anticipate the objection that fractal geometry is not a precise language
choices.tag: Out of Scope: not a precise language
choices.explanation: There's nothing in this first paragraph that seems like it's worried that some people will object to fractal geometry and say, "Hey, that's not a precise language".

choices.text: illustrate the concept of self-similarity
choices.explanation:
This answer is a little surprising, but it's the only eligible answer and the only answer that reinforces language from the first paragraph.

We were looking for "provides some insight into fractal geometry", and the 2nd sentence indicated that fractals commonly exhibit the property of self-similarity.

So we can be at peace with combining these two: the Koch curve was explained in order to provide some insight into how fractals are self-similar.

Through the explanation, we were provided with an example of "the reiteration of irregular details (the pointed protrusion in the middle) at progressively smaller scales".

choices.text: provide an exact definition of fractals
choices.explanation:
The 2nd sentence all but contradicts this, as it says that "an exact definition of fractals has not been established".

The author isn't stepping in to say, "I'll be the hero, everyone. *Here* is the exact definition of fractals."

questions.prompt: Which one of the following does the author present as a characteristic of fractal geometry?

choices.text: It is potentially much more important than calculus.
Its role in traditional mathematics will expand as computers become faster.
It is the fastest-growing field of mathematics.
It encourages the use of computer programs to prove mathematical theorems.
It enables geometers to generate complex forms using simple processes.

questions.prompt: Each of the following statements about the Koch curve can be properly deduced from the information given in the passage EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The Support Window for the keywords *Koch curve* begins in the middle of the 1st paragraph and extends until the end of the 2nd paragraph.

If we had a decent understanding of what we read on our first trip through the passage, we should probably start checking answers, since four of them are supported, so we'll probably remember a couple.

Otherwise, we should "brush up" on what we know about the Koch curve:
- self-similarity (looks the same at any scale)
- significant in math and emblematic of fractal geometry
- follows that script of dividing into 3, then making a triangular protrusion with middle segment.
- result of infinitely many steps, but computer image will be limited at some point

choices.text: The total number of protrusions in the Koch curve at any stage of the construction depends on the length of the initial line chosen for the construction.
choices.explanation: At a given stage, the number of protrusions depends on how many construction steps have been performed, not the absolute initial length. A one-foot and a ten-foot starting line each acquire one protrusion in the first step. Although the limiting curve involves infinitely many steps, the question asks about any stage, where a finite count is meaningful.

choices.text: The line segments at each successive stage of the construction of the Koch curve are shorter than the segments at the previous stage.
choices.explanation:
Since the instructions for making the Koch curve involve taking every line segment you can find and dividing it into three equal parts, as you build this curve, you're dealing with ever-smaller parts.

If you started with a 9 ft line, you'd divide it into three 3 ft. segments.
___ ___ ___
3 3 3
Then you'd copy that middle segment to make a protrusion.

___ / ___
All four of those segments are 3ft. long.

Next, you take each of those 3ft. long segments and chop them into 3rd's.
_ _ _ / ___
1 1 1

At the first stage, we were dealing with 3ft segments. Now we're dealing with 1ft segments. And so on.

choices.text: Theoretically, as the Koch curve is constructed its line segments become infinitely small.
choices.explanation:
In the middle of the 2nd paragraph it says:
*Theoretically, the Koch curve is the result of infinitely many steps in the construction process*.

choices.text: At every stage of constructing the Koch curve, all the line segments composing it are of equal length.
choices.explanation:
As illustrated in the explanation for (B), if you start with a 9 ft. line, then the first stage involves a bunch of 3 ft. segments.

At the second stage, you have all 1 ft. segments. At the third stage, you have all 1/3 ft. segments.

The first paragraph explains:
*one begins with a straight line. The middle third of the line is removed and replaced with two line segments, each as long as the removed piece.*

Because it says "the middle ****third"****, it implies that we have divided the original straight line into thirds, which implies that all three segments are 1/3 the length of the original line. And then the passage explicitly says that the middle third is replaced with two segments that are each as long as the removed middle third.

choices.text: The length of the line segments in the Koch curve at any stage of its construction depends on the length of the initial line chosen for the construction.
choices.explanation:
As we've considered in (B) and (D),

START: 9 ft. line
STAGE 1: 3 ft segments
STAGE 2: 1 ft segments
STAGE 3: 1/3 ft segments

Meanwhile, if we chose a different length of the initial line, we'd have different lengths at corresponding stages.

START: 36 ft. line
STAGE 1: 12 ft segments
STAGE 2: 4 ft segments
STAGE 3: 4/3 ft segments

questions.prompt: The enthusiastic practitioners of fractal geometry mentioned in the first sentence of the third paragraph would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We only have three ideas to represent the point of view of these enthusiastic practitioners:

- fractal geometry is a new language for describing complex natural and mathematical forms
- fractal geometry's significance will rival that of calculus
- a proficiency in fractal geometry will allow mathematicians to describe the form of a cloud as easily and precisely as an architect can describe a house using the language of traditional geometry.

Let's find a safely worded answer that can be supported by one or more of those lines.

choices.text: The Koch curve is the most easily generated, and therefore the most important, of the forms studied by fractal geometers.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most easy / most important
choices.explanation: Nothing in our Support Window is talking about the Koch curve. This is just word-baiting us with stuff from elsewhere in the passage and then adding some extreme words to it, to make it a wrong answer.

choices.text: Fractal geometry will eventually be able to be used in the same applications for which traditional geometry is now used.
choices.explanation: The enthusiasts expect new ability to describe complex natural forms. The passage does not establish that fractal geometry will handle the same applications as traditional geometry. Failure to support shared applications does not require claiming the sets of applications would be identical in every respect.

choices.text: The greatest importance of computer images of fractals is their ability to bring fractal geometry to the attention of a wider public.
choices.explanation:
This is another *word-bait + strong language* answer. The claim right before the highlighted phrase talks about "the public".

But none of our support sentences sound like these geometers think that the ****#1**** reason computer images of fractals are important is that they bring more public attention to fractal geometry.

choices.text: Studying self-similarity was impossible before the development of sophisticated computer technologies.
choices.explanation: Nothing in our supporting sentences sounds like we have never been able to study self-similarity, until this recent development of sophisticated computers.

choices.text: Certain complex natural forms exhibit a type of self-similarity like that exhibited by fractals.
choices.explanation: The opening says fractals commonly exhibit self-similarity. The enthusiasts proposal to describe certain complex natural forms with fractal geometry supports the limited inference that some such forms share that property. We need not claim every fractal or every natural form is self-similar.

questions.prompt: The information in the passage best supports which one of the following assertions?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: There are no keywords. With an *Undefined Target*, we hope to discount some answers on the first pass because of their overly strong language, and then we will try to research the more moderately worded ones.

choices.text: The appeal of a mathematical theory is limited to those individuals who can grasp the theorems and proofs produced in that theory.
choices.tag: Too Strong: limited to / Opposite, if anything
choices.explanation:
This is saying that "only people who can grasp the theorems and proofs produced in a theory can find that theory appealing".

That seems harsh, if not contradicted. The first sentence of the last paragraph is saying that "a worldwide public has become captivated" by fractal geometry". We certainly wouldn't assume that the worldwide public can grasp the theorems and proofs produced in fractal geometry.

choices.text: Most of the important recent breakthroughs in mathematical theory would not have been possible without the ability of computers to graphically represent complex shapes.
choices.tag: Too Strong: most / Opposite, if anything
choices.explanation:
We are always nervous to get as specific as saying **more than 50% of** anything.

Do we know that at least 51% of important recent breakthroughs in math required the ability of computers to graphically represent complex shapes?

Nope. We don't even know of one important breakthrough that required such computers.

choices.text: Fractal geometry holds the potential to replace traditional geometry in most of its engineering applications.
choices.explanation:
Again, this is way too strong/specific. The passage is very cautious in its optimism about fractal geometry. It hasn't proven itself to be especially useful; it's only proven a few theorems that couldn't be proven before.

It's a huge leap to say that it has the potential to replace traditional geometry in **more than 50%** of engineering applications.

choices.text: A mathematical theory can be developed and find applications even before it establishes a precise definition of its subject matter.
choices.explanation: The first paragraph explicitly says an exact definition of fractals has not been established. Yet the passage describes a developed theory, computer-generated constructions and proven theorems. Those supply an example of development and application before a precise definition of the subject. Uncertainty about future uses is different from lacking an exact definition.

choices.text: Only a mathematical theory that supports a system of theorems and proofs will gain enthusiastic support among a significant number of mathematicians.
choices.tag: Too Strong: only / Contradicted, if anything
choices.explanation:
We know that there are already lots of mathematicians who are excited about fractal geometry, despite the fact that the theory isn't yet a precise language supporting a system of theorems and proofs.

But according to this answer, the only way for a theory to gain enthusiastic support is to have a system of theorems and proofs.
